2219277368525613029.title: ეოსი, ძველი ბერძნული განთიადის ქალღმერთი · Eos, Greek Goddess of the Dawn
2219277368525613029.ka_source: წყარო: ეს ქართული ტექსტი ეყრდნობა Greek Reporter-ის სტატიას (greekreporter.com). ილუსტრაციები — იქვე მითითებული მუზეუმებიდან.
2219277368525613029.en:
English summary. The full article is in Georgian — switch to ქა at the top of the page.

Eos is the Greek goddess of the dawn. Hesiod names her a daughter of the Titans Hyperion and Theia, and so a sister of Helios, the Sun, and Selene, the Moon. Homer opens new days in the Iliad and the Odyssey with the same formula: “rosy-fingered Dawn”.

Her myths are mostly stories of love for mortals. She asked Zeus to make Tithonus immortal but forgot to ask for eternal youth, so he aged without end. Their son Memnon, king of the Ethiopians, fell at Troy by the hand of Achilles; later poets said the morning dew is her grief for him. With Astraeus she became mother of the winds and of the stars.

Her name is related to the Vedic dawn goddess Ushas and the Roman Aurora. Linguists reconstruct a common Indo-European dawn goddess behind all three.

Eos is not the day itself. She is the threshold that makes the day possible — a goddess of beginnings who returns every morning and never stays.

Sources

  • Hesiod, Theogony 371–382
  • Homer, Iliad and Odyssey (the “rosy-fingered” formula)
  • Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite 218–238 (Tithonus)
  • Ovid, Metamorphoses XIII (Memnon)

7428074960537347488.title: ძველი ბერძნული ღამის ქალღმერთი ნიქსი · Nyx, Greek Goddess of Night
7428074960537347488.ka_source: წყარო: ეს ქართული ტექსტი ეყრდნობა Greek Reporter-ის სტატიას (greekreporter.com).
7428074960537347488.en:
English summary. The full article is in Georgian — switch to ქა at the top of the page.

Nyx is Night itself, one of the first powers of the Greek cosmos. In Hesiod’s Theogony she is born from Chaos together with Erebus, the darkness below. With Erebus she brings forth Aether, the bright upper air, and Hemera, the Day.

Alone she gives birth to a long line of forces that no one can escape: Sleep and Death, the Dreams, the Fates, Nemesis, Strife and others. Homer shows how much even the gods respect her: in the Iliad, Zeus holds back his anger because he will not offend swift Night.

Nyx had little organised cult, but she has a place in the sky today: the asteroid 3908 Nyx carries her name, and Pluto’s moon Nix was spelled with an “i” to avoid confusion with it.

In Greek thought, Night comes before Day and gives birth to it. Darkness is not the absence of order here — it is the oldest layer of it.

Sources

  • Hesiod, Theogony 123–125, 211–225
  • Homer, Iliad XIV 256–261

5498240519161399952.title: ზევსი, ყველა ღმერთის მეფე ბერძნულ მითოლოგიაში · Zeus, King of the Greek Gods
5498240519161399952.ka_source: წყარო: ეს ქართული ტექსტი ეყრდნობა Greek Reporter-ის სტატიას (greekreporter.com). ილუსტრაციები — იქვე მითითებული მუზეუმებიდან.
5498240519161399952.en:
English summary. The full article is in Georgian — switch to ქა at the top of the page.

Zeus is the king of the Olympian gods: lord of the sky, of thunder and lightning, and guardian of oaths and of guests. He is the son of the Titans Cronus and Rhea. Cronus swallowed his children to keep his throne; Rhea hid the infant Zeus on Crete and gave her husband a stone instead.

Grown, Zeus freed his siblings and, with them, defeated the Titans. The brothers divided the world by lot: Zeus took the sky, Poseidon the sea and Hades the underworld. With Hera as his queen, and through many other unions, Zeus fathered gods and heroes — Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Hermes, Dionysus, Heracles among them.

His great sanctuaries were Olympia, home of the Olympic Games and of Phidias’s gold-and-ivory statue, and Dodona, where his oracle spoke through an oak. His name goes back to the Indo-European sky father, the same root as Vedic Dyaus Pitar and Latin Jupiter.

Zeus is the god of an order that was won, not given: he rules because he ended a cycle of fathers devouring sons.

Sources

  • Hesiod, Theogony 453–506, 617–735
  • Homer, Iliad XV 187–193 (the division of the world)
  • Pausanias, Description of Greece V (Olympia)

101263883423081450.title: ანუ - შუმერის უზენაესი ღმერთი · Anu, Supreme God of Sumer
101263883423081450.ka_source: წყარო: ეს ქართული ტექსტი ეყრდნობა ვიკიპედიის სტატიას „Anu“ (CC BY-SA 4.0); ბიბლიოგრაფია — ტექსტის ბოლოს.
101263883423081450.en:
English summary. The full article is in Georgian — switch to ქა at the top of the page.

An (Sumerian) or Anu (Akkadian) is the sky and the god of the sky — the oldest head of the Mesopotamian pantheon. In cuneiform the same star-shaped sign wrote both his name and the word “god”. He was the source of all authority: kingship and divine rank were said to come from “Anu-ship”.

His great city was Uruk, where the raised White Temple of the fourth millennium BCE is linked to him. His Sumerian consort was Ki, the earth; later texts pair him with Antu. He is father of the Anunnaki, the great gods.

Over time the active rule passed to Enlil and, in Babylon, to Marduk; Anu stayed distant and supreme. In the Epic of Gilgamesh, Ishtar asks him for the Bull of Heaven. His cult returned in Hellenistic Uruk, in the temple called Bit Resh.

Anu shows a pattern seen in many pantheons: the highest god withdraws, and younger gods do the governing in his name.

Sources

  • J. Black, A. Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia (1992)
  • Epic of Gilgamesh, tablet VI
  • Enuma Elish, tablet I

7785409258490098057.title: გლოვა ურისთვის · The Lament for Ur
7785409258490098057.ka_source: წყარო: ეს ქართული ტექსტი ეყრდნობა ვიკიპედიის სტატიებს ღვთაებრივი კრებისა და „Lament for Ur“-ის შესახებ (CC BY-SA 4.0); ბიბლიოგრაფია — ტექსტის ბოლოს.
7785409258490098057.en:
English summary. The full article is in Georgian — switch to ქა at the top of the page.

The Lament for Ur is a Sumerian city lament, written in the early second millennium BCE after the fall of Ur around 2004 BCE, when the last dynasty of Ur was overthrown by the Elamites and their allies.

In the poem the goddess Ningal, wife of Ur’s moon god Nanna, weeps before the assembly of the gods, An and Enlil at its head, and begs them to spare her city. The assembly has already decided. Enlil sends a storm, the city falls, and Ningal is left to mourn among the ruins. The text is arranged in eleven songs.

The lament survives on Old Babylonian clay tablets, mainly from Nippur and Ur. It belongs to a small group of Sumerian city laments, alongside the laments for Sumer and Ur, Nippur, Eridu and Uruk.

The poem turns a political defeat into a cosmic decree: Ur did not fall because it was weak, but because the gods’ assembly ruled so. History becomes memory through that change.

Sources

  • N. Samet, The Lament over the Destruction of Ur (2014)
  • S. N. Kramer, Lamentation over the Destruction of Ur (1940)
  • Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature (ETCSL), text 2.2.2
